## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Soṇakajātaka* (Ja 529) is a narrative in the Pali Jātaka collection, rendered in English as *Prince Arindama and His Friend Soṇaka* [SuttaCentral]. The canonical commentary sets the introductory framing narrative at Jetavana, where the Buddha addresses the assembly on the Perfection of Renunciation (*nekkhammapāramī*), observing that he accomplished the Great Renunciation in earlier births as well [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1891]. In the narrative of the past, set in Rājagaha, the Bodhisatta was born as King Arindama, whose companion was Soṇaka [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1891]. In the Jātaka's conclusion, Soṇaka attains enlightenment as a Paccekabuddha, King Arindama is identified as the Bodhisatta, and his son is identified as the future Prince Rāhula [Fausböll 1891].

Scholarly analysis highlights the narrative's exploration of possessionlessness: it sets the opulence of royal rule against the homeless life of the wanderer, demonstrating the spiritual insufficiency of sovereign power [Fenn 1994]. In the dialogue between the king and the renouncer, poverty is listed among the virtues and blessings of renunciation, serving as a catalyst for the monarch's abdication and adoption of the ascetic life [Fenn 1994].

A full parallel to the narrative is preserved in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit in the *Mahāvastu-avadāna* under the title *The Jātaka of Arindama* (Mvu 111) [SuttaCentral], a relationship strongly supported by DharmaNexus text-matching with 94 aligned segments [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral also notes passage-level parallels with the *Mūgapakkhajātaka* (Ja 538) and *Soṇanandajātaka* (Ja 532), alongside thematic parallels with the *Mahājanakajātaka* (Ja 539) and the *Saṁghavandanāsutta* (SN 11.20) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus identifies extensive Pali-internal verse and prose reuse across the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Mahājanakajātaka* (Ja 539), the *Vessantarajātaka* (Ja 547), and several poems in the *Apadāna* (notably Tha-Ap 410, Tha-Ap 413, and Tha-Ap 487) [DharmaNexus].
